name: Wei Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to any company, union, party or government, and your answers stay confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a loader underground at the gold mine, the low, long machine that scoops broken ore from the stopes and carries it to the ore pass. I'm the lead operator on my crew, so I set the order of the headings and sort out problems on the radio. Two of our loaders already run tele-remote, someone drives them from the surface through shift change while we're coming up. I like the problem-solving, figuring out how to clear a hang-up without anyone getting hurt. What wears me out is the overtime they cut last year, because that was our margin.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hana's a nurse at the district hospital, on rotating shifts, so we juggle the kids like a relay race. Our son's fifteen and our daughter's nine. The mortgage takes most of my pay, and since the overtime went we've got about two weeks of slack. In my spare time I fix lawnmowers and small engines in the garage, mostly for neighbours, mostly for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, everyone calm down. At work I'd joke that the AI still can't find a hang-up in a drawpoint. I don't post much, maybe a thumbs-up on someone else's post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, fine by me. I use the chatbot now and then for my son's maths homework, and that's useful enough. The tele-remote loaders were coming anyway, AI or not, so my real question doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd ask again about getting the overtime back, through the union rep, and maybe start charging the neighbours a bit for the mower repairs. Twenty dollars a job adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit like a quiet shift, nothing to report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tele-remote loaders were coming anyway. What's your question about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether they put me on one of those surface seats or leave me underground till the end. I've driven the remote one twice when the regular guy was sick. It's like a video game, except the game costs four million dollars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the surface seat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part of me, yes, no dust, no heat, home on time. Part of me would miss the feel of the machine, you know when the bucket's full by how it rocks. I'd take it, though, once I saw the others weren't miserable up there.

S0.say: I'd tell people to calm down and joke that AI still can't find a hang-up in a drawpoint. Online I'd do little more than give someone else's post a thumbs-up.
S0.think: Privately it's fine by me, since I only use the chatbot for my son's homework. The tele-remote loaders were coming anyway, so my real question stays the same.
S0.do: Carries on as usual and asks the union rep again about restoring overtime. Starts charging neighbours around twenty dollars per mower repair.
S0.feel: Calm, like a quiet shift with nothing to report.
S0.quote: It's like a video game, except the game costs four million dollars.
S0.fieldNote: Wei separates AI hype from the remote loaders already at his mine. He's open to the surface seat but wants to see colleagues settle in first, which fits his steady nature. The mower repairs are a small, real idea for extra income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a change, and the smart thing is to get trained early rather than complain. I'd say the company should train from within, because we know the mine. I'd say both, really, fair to everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think they'd go to mostly tele-remote loading within a few years, with one person running two or three machines. Some of us get the surface seats, most don't. I've got a decent shot because I've already driven it, but decent isn't certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor for the remote training in the first month, once I'd seen how the first group got on. I'd get the mower repairs going properly as a weekend thing. And we'd drop the second phone plan and the streaming, small stuff, maybe sixty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd be watching every notice on the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said once you'd seen how the first group got on. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first group always finds the problems. Like the guy who went to the remote room early and found the screens gave him headaches, they fixed it six months later. I'm not first through the door, but I'm not last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hana say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say go for it, she's always been braver than me. And her job's safer than mine, nursing isn't going anywhere fast. That's the comfort, really, one of us is solid.

S1.say: I'd say the smart move is to get trained early rather than complain. I'd also say the company should train from within, because existing crews know the mine.
S1.think: I really think most loading goes tele-remote within a few years, with one person running several machines. I have a decent shot at a surface seat because I've driven one, but it isn't certain.
S1.do: Asks his supervisor for remote training in the first month, after watching the first group. Turns mower repairs into a weekend business and cuts the second phone plan and streaming, about sixty a month.
S1.feel: Uneasy, watching every notice on the board.
S1.quote: I'm not first through the door, but I'm not last either.
S1.fieldNote: Wei describes his own steady approach almost word for word: let others find the problems, then follow fast. His partner's nursing job gives him a sense of a floor under the family. He favours fairness to workers and company alike, typical of his middle-ground views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening too fast for anyone to cope, and the government and the companies should agree on a slower rollout or proper support. I'd say it without shouting, though people would be shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the surface seats go too, because the AI drives the loader itself, no person needed. So in a year or so I'm out. We'd lean on Hana's pay, but her pay alone doesn't cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Hana the first weekend and go through every bill. We'd tell the bank early and ask about interest-only for a year. I'd push the mower business hard, and look at whether the hospital needs maintenance people, because hospitals still need things fixed by a person, for a while anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said nursing isn't going anywhere fast. Does that still hold in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to believe it, but if robots can drive a loader in a stope, maybe they can lift patients too. Hana says people want a person holding their hand. I hope she's right, because it's our whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's fifteen and thinking about an apprenticeship at the mine, like me. I'd tell him to wait, maybe look at something with people, not machines. That would be a hard talk, because he's proud of what I do.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to cope, and government and companies should agree on a slower rollout or proper support. I'd say it calmly while others shouted.
S2.think: I think the surface seats go too, because AI drives the loader itself, so I'd be out in about a year. We'd lean on Hana's pay, but it can't cover the mortgage alone.
S2.do: Goes through every bill with Hana on the first weekend and asks the bank about a year of interest-only payments. Pushes the mower business and looks for maintenance work at the hospital.
S2.feel: Alarmed and lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: Hana says people want a person holding their hand. I hope she's right, because it's our whole plan.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture removes Wei's remote-seat option and pushes the family onto his partner's income. When pressed, he admitted that even nursing might not be safe, which shook him. He'd steer his son away from a mining apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if we start now, and the mine and the government should lay out what jobs are coming and train people for them. That's the reasonable middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get maybe three years in a surface seat, which is good money compared to nothing. After that I'd need something else, and I'd want to have started it already. Small engines, maybe, or the hospital maintenance idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the remote training in year one, once the first group was through. In year two I'd start a night course in building maintenance or electrical. We'd save whatever the surface job adds, aiming for two months of bills by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It's a plan with steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment you imagine, when you'd know it's time to move on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they put a second loader on my screen. That's the sign they're thinning us out. I'd want to be halfway through the new course by then, not starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up for the night course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fishing on Sunday mornings with my brother-in-law, probably. That one hurts, it's the only time I'm not thinking about anything. But it's a few years, not forever.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan if we start now, with the mine and government laying out coming jobs and training for them. I'd call that the reasonable middle.
S3.think: I think I'd get about three good years in a surface seat before needing something else. I'd want the next thing already started, such as small engines or hospital maintenance.
S3.do: Takes remote training in year one after the first group, then a night course in building maintenance or electrical in year two. Saves the extra surface pay, aiming for two months of bills by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a manageable way, with a plan in steps.
S3.quote: When they put a second loader on my screen. That's the sign they're thinning us out.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Wei builds a sensible staged plan and even names the signal he'd watch for. He is willing to give up his Sunday fishing, a small but telling sacrifice. His mood eases from alarmed to a working kind of anxiety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people use it, so no excuses from anyone, workers included. I'd say the company should commit to training and people should actually turn up to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years is close to fine for me. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be through school, and I'd have had time to move into maintenance properly. I'd still be a bit sad about the loader, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the remote training when it comes, and start the maintenance certificate in a year or two, at an easy pace. I'd build the mower business slowly into something real, maybe rent a small unit by year five. And we'd put a bit away each month, which we've honestly never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the normal kind. Like knowing the car needs new tyres next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said workers should turn up to the training. Do you think many wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some wouldn't. With ten years, plenty of guys would say, I'll deal with it later. I'd be tempted too, if I'm honest, that's how people are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your advice to your son change with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Maybe he does the apprenticeship as an electrician, which is useful in a mine and out of it. I'd want him to have something he can carry to another town.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty if people use it, so there's no excuse for anyone, workers included. The company should commit to training and people should actually attend.
S4.think: I think ten years is close to fine for me: I'd be fifty-three with the kids through school and time to move into maintenance. I'd still feel a bit sad about leaving the loader.
S4.do: Takes the remote training when offered and starts a maintenance certificate at an easy pace within two years. Grows the mower business slowly, maybe renting a unit by year five, and saves a little each month.
S4.feel: Uneasy in an ordinary way, like knowing the car will need new tyres next year.
S4.quote: I'd want him to have something he can carry to another town.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years fits Wei's steady pace and his life stage, so his worry becomes routine. He admitted he might be tempted to delay himself. His advice to his son shifts towards a trade that travels, such as electrical work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the remote seat disappears before I can even sit in it. What would help is the bank giving miners a year of reduced payments during a changeover, and paid training before the layoffs, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about safety. Half of what a lead operator does is keeping people alive underground. If there are fewer people down there, that's good, but the last few would be very alone.

headlineQuote: If there are fewer people down there, that's good, but the last few would be very alone.
portrait: Wei Nakamura is a 43-year-old lead loader operator at an underground gold mine, married to a hospital nurse, with a teenage son, a young daughter, a mortgage and about two weeks of slack since overtime was cut. He fixes lawnmowers on the side and uses AI only now and then. He is calm if AI stalls and uneasy under steady change, planning to follow colleagues into tele-remote seats once they've proven them. The two-year AGI picture alarms him because it removes even those seats and leaves the family leaning on his partner's pay, while five or ten years let him build a staged move into maintenance work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the remote operating seat would vanish before he could take it.
whatWouldHelp: A year of reduced mortgage payments during a changeover, and paid training before layoffs rather than after.
